Title: Denver Barkey hoping to be center of attention for Flyers
People: Sean Couturier,1338;Trevor Zegras,1321;Christian Dvorak,1357;Denver Barkey,37;Rick Tocchet,2990;Logan Stankoven,2531
Article_Text:
VOORHEES, N.J. – Denver Barkey made the move from wing to center for a couple of Flyers playoff games last year due to an injury to Noah Cates.
All of 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds, Barkey liked it so much and played well enough that he could wind up there when the season gets underway on Sept. 30.
Barkey is quick enough and light enough on his skates to make up for his lack of size. His hockey IQ is through the roof, which can help keep him out of trouble. He played center in junior in London, Ontario, at age 16. So it’s not a completely overwhelming transition.
“It takes a lot of work to be an established NHL centerman,” Barkey said after Saturday’s intrasquad scrimmage at the Flyers Training Center. “One thing I’ve always taken pride in is being a versatile player, someone who can play center or wing.”
Barkey says whatever experience he lacks at center can be made up by studying a lot of video.
“I know the task at hand, what a centerman needs to do in all three zones through the game,” he said. “Having the opportunity to show them I can play center and hold my own is just another opportunity for me. Looking to run away with it.”
A meeting with the coaching staff over the summer laid the groundwork for the potential switch.
The Flyers don’t have a desperate need in the middle. They already have Trevor Zegras, Sean Couturier, Christian Dvorak and Cates at that position.
“They (the coaches) let me know they like how I played at center in those two playoff games,” the 21-year-old Newmarket, Ont. native said. “I wasn’t out of place sort of thing. I worked on things over the summer that are going to help me excel at that position.”
Barkey only posted 17 points in 43 regular-season games last year, but that could change if he finds himself between a couple talented wingers.
One player Barkey is sure to consult with is Couturier, the Flyers captain who is the dean of Philadelphia professional athletes.
“If I continue to stay there (at center), Coots will be a big one,” Barkey said. “Pick the brain of him … Selke (Trophy) winner, someone who knows how to play the game the right way. He plays the offensive side of the puck and the defensive side of the puck very well.
“He’s just a guy you can put out there in any situation and rely on him. I’ll work with him after practice. See if he has some pointers to help me out.”
A lot of NHL centers go around 6-foot-3 and about 200 pounds. Barkey is far from that, but it won’t stop him from achieving his goal once he sets his mind to it. Carolina playoff hero Logan Stankoven (5-foot-8, 165 pounds) is a good example of overcoming a size deficiency
“Over the years you’ve seen more and more guys be able to have a big impact on this league,” Barkey said. “He (Stankoven) is only 5-8, 5-9 and yet he made a huge impact in all three zones. He did a lot of things a lot of people probably didn’t think he could do. He won a lot of puck battles and he wasn’t afraid. That’s someone I try to keep a close eye on. Stature-wise, we’re pretty similar.”
Coach Rick Tocchet believes Barkey has what it takes to make the switch, if that’s the direction the team opts for.
“There’s something there we have to look at,” Tocchet said. “He’s a smart guy. I don’t think he hurts you defensively. So that (move) is something we’re going to have to look into.”

Title: In the pink: Painting the Planet Pink for cancer research, awareness
People: Sabatini Bottleshop,6857;Barbara Sciandra,4039;Barbara Sciandra,5407;Shaun Daney,1357;Shaun Daney,1551;Russell Keeler,509;Russell Keeler,581;Russell Keeler,2072;Russell Keeler,2239;Russell Keeler,3362;Russell Keeler,6076;Mason Gross,713;Mason Gross,862;Mason Gross,2104;Mason Gross,2271;Mason Gross,2307;Mason Gross,2484;Christopher Hughes,18;Dino Galella,1341;Dino Galella,1535;Ashley Hules,1573;Ashley Hules,1810;John Joyce,2735;John Joyce,2900;Anthony Macario,1878;Anthony Macario,2016;Paige Cognetti,943;Paige Cognetti,1107;Ed Ackerman,5881;Qiana Lehman,4054;Bridget Malloy Kosierowski,1040;Aliah Hughes,467;Aliah Hughes,3177;Aliah Hughes,3311;Aliah Hughes,3528;John Dolphin,2956;John Dolphin,3111
Organizations: University Of Pennsylvania,4225;University Of Pennsylvania,4795;Walkers,1148;Walkers,1262;Maria Goretti Church Banquet Hall,6777
Article_Text:
Christopher Hughes, of Archbald, stepped up to the starting line at Saturday’s Paint the Planet Pink 5K with a victory already in hand.
Hughes’ real win came not with an especially stellar time or placement on the leaderboard, but in his wife Aliah’s successful battle against breast cancer.
Both came to the Paint the Planet Pink event decked in pink and determined to help raise money and awareness so others can have the benefit of research and treatment that Aliah Hughes believes saved her life.
Diagnosed in 2024 at only 35 years old, Aliah Hughes points out that women seem to be diagnosed younger and younger.
The Paint the Planet Pink events, geared toward fundraising for cancer research, make overcoming the disease possible, she said.
A tradition and a commitment
Paint the Planet Pink graced Scranton’s downtown not simply as an event, but as a tradition—a gathering of friends, families, and survivors united by memories, hope, and a commitment to support breast cancer research.
The series of events is the brainchild of Barbara Sciandra and Qiana Lehman, who organized a three-day fundraiser in 2014. It has since grown into a regional tradition dedicated to raising money for cancer research at the University of Pennsylvania.
Sciandra founded the initiative to support research into an immunotherapy treatment that she credits with saving her life after her 2012 breast cancer diagnosis.
In 2024, the organization introduced a new logo and rebranded to Paint the Planet Pink, moving its 5K race, walk, and Gentlemen’s Dash to Scranton. Despite the shift, Sciandra emphasizes that multiple events remain anchored in Luzerne County, backed by strong regional support.
Over its first 12 years, the effort raised $1 million for cancer research at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. Yet as Sciandra looked out on a sea of pink Saturday, what she saw most vividly were the faces—returning supporters who have attended since day one alongside new faces eager to learn about breast cancer research and to contribute.
Balancing event preparation with a busy home life isn’t easy, especially as her three children grow toward adulthood and take on numerous activities. But Sciandra stays driven by her deep commitment to her family and to others facing cancer.
Running like men – in heels
The Gentlemen’s Dash is the brainchild of Barbara Sciandra’s husband, Sal.
After the event’s first season in 2014, the couple was discussing ideas for future fundraising events. Sal came up with the idea of men in high heels racing down Main Street. He believed that his idea would serve as a symbol of the pain that women, and even men, face while undergoing cancer treatment.
Now, it is a top fundraiser and a favorite of those attending the event. Sciandra remembers back to the event’s inaugural season, when she called Ed Ackerman and asked him if he would participate.
Ackerman didn’t really know what he was agreeing to, but simply said a quick, “yes.”
He got to run in flats that year, she said, laughing.
Russell Keeler also ran in that first Gentlemen’s Dash and was back to give it another try Saturday.
He purchased his size 15 high heels on Amazon, with a thicker heel he hoped would provide a little stability to his steps.
Keeler’s goal wasn’t to finish first, but to simply make it down the street without falling, he said.
The real win, he said, was the fundraising the event provides. The window for voting for a favorite dasher runs until Oct. 3.
Upcoming events
Although the 5K, family run and Gentlemen’s Dash are among the best-known events of the Paint the Planet Pink effort, the fun and fundraising aren’t over yet.
On the schedule are a cash and purse bingo on Sunday, Sept. 27, at St. Maria Goretti Church Banquet Hall in Laflin; ’90s trivia night and meat raffle on Tuesday, Sept. 29, at Sabatini’s Bottleshop in Exeter; and Paint the Red Mill Pink, a guest bartender happy hour, on Saturday, Oct. 3, at the Red Mill in Pittston.
Details, tickets, and donation options are available at painttheplanetpink.org.
